GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: Precipitation chances continue into Friday afternoon, though coverage will gradually taper off. Meanwhile, the low pressure system will be absorbed into the main flow, driving a frontal passage through the area.
GJT.text:
ISOLATED SHOWERS AND SEASONABLE TEMPS TO BEGIN THE WORK WEEK:

Broad southwesterly flow will dominate the start of the work week, maintaining moisture advection across the region. Expect a continuation of cloud cover along with isolated showers through Tuesday. Modest warm air advection will nudge high temperatures closer to seasonal normals despite the increased cloud cover. While localized breezy conditions could accompany collapsing showers, organized convection is not anticipated.

WIDESPREAD RAIN AND FLOOD POTENTIAL LATE-WEEK:

By Wednesday, a strong low pressure system drops southward along the California coast, while an upper level jet noses into the Four Corners region. These two features will work in tandem to bring remnant moisture from what is now Hurricane Trudy into the region, bringing the return of widespread precipitation chances. Initial model solutions depict the most likely time period for widespread showers to be Wednesday night through Thursday night. It is also important to note that a large majority of the precipitation from this system will fall as rain, with the pool of colder temperatures staying well north of the forecast area. As a result, snow levels will remain high, generally at or above 12,000 feet. Given the prospect of high-elevation rain falling onto antecedent snowpack and saturated soils from last week's precipitation, flash flooding and hydrologic impacts will be monitored closely as the system progresses. The highest amounts of rainfall are currently showing up in the southern mountains where 1-3 inches of rainfall are possible. The San Juans look to take the brunt from this system so locally higher amounts are possible. In fact, some of the river forecasts in that area are reaching flood stage. Ensemble guidance supports PWATs upwards of 250-300% of normal, providing another strong signal to monitor for potential impacts. Keep in mind that the forecast remains fluid this far out, and key details may shift over the coming days.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: Regarding temperatures, there is pretty good agreement in temperatures staying warmer than seasonable through at least Saturday, with the Denver metro and plains potentially reaching the mid to upper 70s Wednesday through Friday.
BOU.text:
Current observations show temperatures in the 50s and 60s, and mostly sunny skies east of the Continental Divide. A few showers have developed over western Colorado and parts of Park County, although these should be short-lived. Decreasing cloud cover over the mountains and clear skies for the plains late tonight will give way to one more chilly morning (though still above average) with morning lows in the upper 30s to low 40s across the low elevations, and 30s for the mountains.

Tomorrow, a shortwave will continue to drift through the area and allow for a few light showers over the high terrain once again in the afternoon. For the plains and Denver metro, 70-degree afternoon highs make a return with a few patches of mid level clouds and perhaps some virga. Surface winds are expected to generally remain light at all levels through at least tomorrow evening due to the weak pressure gradient and light southwest flow aloft.

The synoptic pattern becomes more amplified on Wednesday as an upper level ridge builds over just east of our area and a strong cutoff low approaches the California coast. A subtropical jet ahead of this cutoff low will strengthen southwesterly flow aloft and begin advecting Pacific moisture towards the Four Corners Wednesday evening into Thursday. This increase in moisture will allow rain showers to become more numerous over the mountains Wednesday evening, although the heaviest rain should remain well outside of our CWA, over southwest Colorado. In terms of rainfall amounts, a trace up to 0.25" of QPF seems reasonable for the mountains, with the Denver metro and plains remaining dry. The airmass appears to be too warm for any tangible snow accumulations, with perhaps only some dustings above 12,000 ft. It is worth noting that moisture transport with this system is quite impressive. PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Further east, with the transitory ridge, warm and mainly dry conditions will be in place, with chances of showers spreading east across the plains in later Thursday, as the Pacific system lifts out across the Northern Rockies.
PUB.text:
Latest operational and ensemble model data remain in good agreement through the end of the work week, with transitory upper ridging building across eastern Colorado through Thursday, as southwest flow increases across western Colorado ahead of an eastern Pacific storm system digging into the Great Basin. Model data supports abundant sup-tropical moisture becoming entrained within the southwest flow aloft, with PWATS of 0.8 to over 1 inch (200-300 percent of normal) moving across the region in the Wednesday and Thursday timeframe. This, along with increasing orographic flow, and uvv associated with the Pacific system moving across the Great Basin, will lead to increasing coverage and intensity of precipitation along and west of the Continental Divide Wednesday, with the heaviest precipitation expected Thursday into Thursday night, as the main system starts to lift out across the Great Basin into the Northern Rockies.

Latest model data continues to support qpf of 1 to 3 inches along and west of the ContDvd through this period, with probabilities of >3 inches of liquid qpf in the 60 to 80 percent range across the San Juan Mtns. The Pacific origin of the system is expected to keep snow levels around peak level (at and above 12,000 feet) through the duration of the heavy precipitation event (at least through Thursday night), leading to concerns of river and stream flooding as well as the potential for rock/mudslides across the higher terrain of the ContDvd. However, the area of greatest concern remains across the San Juan Mtns, with already saturated soils from previous precipitation last week, as well the potential for rain on top of snowpack already in place, with SNOTEL data indicating SWE 3/4 to 1" across the San Juans at this time. Stay tuned for more information on this potentially high impact event unfolding later this week, with Flood Watches likely being issued as we get closer in time to this heavy precipitation event.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Sunday/Monday...Drier conditions return under northwest flow aloft and as the low and mid levels dry out somewhat. 700 mb temperatures near 3 Celsius will yield high temperatures in the mid 50s to lower 60s.
CYS.text:
Wednesday...Westerly flow aloft continues and with dry low and mid levels, no precipitation is expected.

Thursday...Moist south southwest flow aloft develops in advance of the upper low over Nevada, with deeper moisture and a weak shortwave trough aloft moving across our western counties, producing scattered showers and a few thunderstorms south of a line from Rawlins, to Wheatland to Cheyenne.

Friday...As the main trough aloft moves across western Wyoming, a cold front will lie north to south across our counties, helping to produce scattered showers mainly west of I-25 in the afternoon, and spreading eastward in the evening.

Saturday...The primary trough aloft moves overhead early in the day, and orographic lift will likely produce scattered showers in the afternoon from Douglas to Laramie, and in the evening south of a Rawlins to Scottsbluff line.

Sunday/Monday...Drier conditions return under northwest flow aloft and as the low and mid levels dry out somewhat. 700 mb temperatures near 3 Celsius will yield high temperatures in the mid 50s to lower 60s.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Beyond Friday, there continues to be some model spread with the large-scale pattern. In general, however, there looks to be a drying and warming trend over Utah continues through early next week.
SLC.text:
Remnants of a weakening storm system continues to lift across Arizona into the Four Corners area today. With lingering moisture in place, weak forcing and very modest instability should be enough to maintain some generally weak showers through the rest of the day across mainly the higher terrain of southern and central Utah (with possibly a couple of thunderstorms in southwest Utah).

Tomorrow into Wednesday, expect southwesterly flow to progressively increase over Utah as a closed low slowly slides down the California coast. This southwesterly flow will maintain temperatures generally above climatological normals across the area. As instability increases tomorrow along with some developing upper diffluence, expect a slight increase in shower coverage and thunderstorm potential, focused primarily over the spine of Utah and western Utah.

By Wednesday afternoon, a jet nosing into southern Utah will be accompanied by a plume of moisture with origins near what is currently Tropical Storm Trudy. The bulk of this moisture looks to cross the southeastern portions of the forecast area. Additionally, the latest deterministic models are now a bit faster with the onset of precipitation on Wednesday compared to other recent runs. As such, expect precipitation to increase from the south on Wednesday, then become more widespread across the forecast area on Thursday as the storm system moves inland. Locally moderate to heavy precipitation can be expected, with a threat of flash flooding especially in prone areas of southern and central Utah. There is currently a Slight Risk of excessive rainfall for southern Utah Wednesday and Thursday. The NBM indicates a broad area of 1 to 2.5 inches of QPF extending from far southwest Utah through southeast and east-central Utah. Elsewhere, the NBM has up to 1 inch except around 1.5 inches in the Uintas. BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: Pattern uncertainty increases behind this system, however Saturday at the very least should be dry with temperatures warming to near normal again.
BOI.text:
Widespread showers will be the story Thursday into Friday, as the low lifts northeast over our area from California. While cloud cover will help limit daytime instability, cooling aloft will allow for weak instability to develop, resulting in a slight chance of embedded thunderstorms. Any thunderstorms will result in localized heavier rainfall rates/totals underneath the core. At least for Thursday, southerly flow aloft will keep snow levels on the higher side (9-10kft MSL), giving rain its opportunity to shine as the dominate precipitation type. Over the course of Thursday through Friday, guidance continues to trend upwards on total accumulations, with lower elevations ranging from 0.15-0.50 inches (lowest in eastern Oregon), mountain valleys ranging from 0.50-0.80 inches, and highest elevations up to 1.25 inches; with the bulk of the precipitation falling late Thursday into early Friday. While this will be more stratiform and long duration in nature, steep terrain/burn scars may experience increased runoff and land movement.

A cold front on Friday will bring a rather sharp end to the precip and a cooldown as it moves across our area from west to east. Temperatures comes Friday will drop around 5 degrees below normal. Another, probably more notable, consequence of the cold front will be the gusty west-northwest winds that will accompany it. Friday afternoon, winds across ridge tops and open terrain will gust to 20- 35 mph. The strongest winds, however, will blow in the Snake River Plain east of Mountain Home where gusts will reach 35-45 mph. Lowering snow levels on Friday behind the front will allow for a transition to snow/wintry mix for elevations above 6.5 kft MSL. Although this switch will be at the tail end of the precipitation, so only a dusting of snow is expected along high elevation passes such as Banner Summit.
